questions.stem: The Nile flows from south to north. Upper Egypt therefore refers to:
options: the Nile Delta in the north
the Western Desert oases
the Sinai Peninsula in the east
the Nile Valley in the south
questions.explanation: Upper and Lower refer to the flow of the river: Upper Egypt is upstream, in the south, and Lower Egypt is the Delta in the north, where the Nile reaches the Mediterranean.

questions.stem: Egyptians called the fertile land along the Nile ‘Kemet’, meaning:
options: ‘the two lands’
‘the land of the god’
‘the black land’
‘the red land’
questions.explanation: Kemet, the black land, referred to the dark silt left by the flood. The desert on either side was Deshret, the red land. ‘The Two Lands’ was a name for Upper and Lower Egypt together.

questions.stem: Why did agriculture in Upper Egypt depend completely on the Nile flood?
options: Upper Egypt drew all of its water from deep wells in the desert
Upper Egypt received almost no rain, unlike the Delta in the north
Upper Egypt had heavy rain every winter that washed away its fields
Upper Egypt grew only crops that needed the soil to stay underwater
questions.explanation: Rainfall in Upper Egypt was close to nothing, so crops grew only where the flood and irrigation reached. The Delta receives far more rain than the south, though it too relied on the flood.

questions.stem: The Egyptian year was divided into three seasons. Akhet was the season when:
options: the Nile flooded the fields
the crops were harvested
the seeds began to sprout
the river was at its lowest
questions.explanation: Akhet was the inundation, from about July to October. Peret was the season of growing, when the fields emerged from the water, and Shemu was harvest time, when the river was low.

questions.stem: Unlike Mesopotamia, Egypt was rarely threatened by its neighbours for much of its early history. Which geographical feature best explains this?
options: Deserts on either side of the valley and cataracts on the Nile to the south
Thick forests along the Mediterranean coast that blocked any landing
High mountain ranges running the length of the Nile Valley on both of its banks
A wide sea that separated the Nile Valley from every other kingdom
questions.explanation: The Eastern and Western deserts and the rocky cataracts of the upper Nile made invasion difficult, so Egypt could develop in relative isolation. Egypt has no mountain ranges along the valley, and its Delta coast was not forested.

questions.stem: The Nile was central to Egypt's economy and unity mainly because it:
options: carried boats north with the current and south with the wind
formed a barrier that kept Upper Egypt apart from Lower Egypt
flooded so violently that it could not be used for travel
flowed only through the Delta and dried up in the south
questions.explanation: The current carried boats north, and the prevailing wind from the north let them sail back south, so the river linked the whole country for trade, tribute and government. It joined, rather than divided, the two lands.

questions.stem: Egypt had good local supplies of which resource used in its monuments?
options: Tin for making bronze tools
Silver for royal jewellery
Limestone and granite for building
Cedar timber for building large ships
questions.explanation: Limestone from the Nile cliffs and granite from Aswan gave Egypt abundant building stone. Cedar for ships came from Byblos in the Levant, and tin and silver were imported.

questions.stem: During the Predynastic Period, the leading centres of Upper Egypt included:
options: Thebes, Karnak and Luxor
Avaris, Buto, Tanis and Alexandria
Hierakonpolis, Naqada and Abydos
Memphis, Giza and Saqqara
questions.explanation: Hierakonpolis (Nekhen), Naqada and Abydos were the main Upper Egyptian centres before unification. Memphis was founded at the junction of the two lands around the time of unification, and Alexandria was founded much later by Alexander the Great.

questions.stem: Archaeologists see the spread of Naqada pottery and burial styles northward into the Delta as evidence that:
options: the two regions had no contact until the reign of King Djoser
Upper Egyptian culture expanded north before political unification
Lower Egyptian culture spread south and replaced that of the Naqada
the Delta was empty of settlement until the first dynasty began
questions.explanation: Naqada material culture gradually replaced the local Lower Egyptian (Buto-Maadi) culture, suggesting Upper Egypt's influence was spreading north. Whether this was by conquest, trade or both is debated. The Delta had long been settled.

questions.stem: Which reason for the expansion of Upper Egypt is best supported by historians?
options: Heavy rains in the south that made farming there impossible
Competition among southern centres for trade, resources and prestige
A sudden invasion of the south by a people from across the Red Sea
Pressure from Mesopotamian armies that had conquered the Delta
questions.explanation: Upper Egyptian centres competed for control of trade routes, gold and prestige goods, and the strongest absorbed their rivals before moving north. No invasion from Mesopotamia occurred, and the south had almost no rain.

questions.stem: The double crown of Egypt combined:
options: the red crown of Upper Egypt and the white crown of Lower Egypt
the blue crown of war and the gold crown of the sun god Re
the crown of the living king and the crown of the god Osiris
the white crown of Upper Egypt and the red crown of Lower Egypt
questions.explanation: The white crown stood for Upper Egypt and the red crown for Lower Egypt; worn together they showed rule over both lands. Egyptians thought of completeness as made of two parts, so the king was ‘Lord of the Two Lands’.

questions.stem: Which ruler is usually regarded by historians as the first to unite Upper and Lower Egypt?
options: Djoser
Khufu
Mentuhotep II
Narmer
questions.explanation: Narmer, an Upper Egyptian king, is usually seen as the first to rule both lands, around the start of the First Dynasty. Mentuhotep II reunified Egypt much later, after the First Intermediate Period.

questions.stem: The Narmer Palette was found by James Quibell and Frederick Green in the 1890s at:
options: Deir el-Medina
Memphis
Hierakonpolis
Giza
questions.explanation: The palette came from the temple area at Hierakonpolis, an important Upper Egyptian centre linked to the falcon god Horus. It is now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

questions.stem: On one side of the Narmer Palette the king wears the white crown and strikes a kneeling enemy. On the other side he wears:
options: no crown at all, kneeling in prayer before the god Re
the red crown, in a procession towards rows of beheaded bodies
the double crown, seated on a throne between the gods Osiris and Re
the blue war crown, driving a horse chariot into battle
questions.explanation: The reverse shows Narmer wearing the red crown of Lower Egypt and inspecting decapitated enemies. Showing him in both crowns is why the palette is linked to unification. Horse chariots were not used in Egypt until about 1,500 years later.

questions.stem: Some historians argue that the Narmer Palette records a real war of unification; others see it as a ceremonial object showing the king's ideal role. Which point best supports the second view?
options: It was found at Hierakonpolis, an important centre of Upper Egypt
It names Narmer with hieroglyphic signs at the top of each side
It uses a stock image of the king smiting enemies, repeated for millennia
It shows Narmer wearing the crowns of both Upper Egypt and Lower Egypt in turn
questions.explanation: The smiting scene became a timeless image of kingship repeated on temple walls for thousands of years, which suggests the palette shows the ideal of royal power over chaos rather than a single event. The crowns and name support identification, not the ritual reading.

questions.stem: On the Narmer Palette, the falcon Horus holds a rope tied to a human head emerging from papyrus plants. Historians usually read this as:
options: a record of the papyrus harvest in Upper Egypt
a scene from a festival of the moon god at Thebes
the king, as Horus, subduing the people of the Delta
the king's offering of papyrus to the god of the dead
questions.explanation: Papyrus was the emblem of the Delta, and the falcon represents Horus, with whom the king was identified. The image is read as Narmer conquering Lower Egypt.

questions.stem: Egyptian hieroglyphs first came into use around the time of:
options: the reign of Mentuhotep II, after the reunification
the Hyksos rule from the city of Avaris
the late Predynastic and Early Dynastic periods
the building of the Great Pyramid at Giza
questions.explanation: The earliest hieroglyphs appear on labels and objects from the late Predynastic and Early Dynastic periods, before 3000 BCE. By the time of the Giza pyramids, writing had been in use for centuries.

questions.stem: The Rosetta Stone allowed scholars to decipher hieroglyphs because it carries:
options: the same decree in hieroglyphic, demotic and Greek
a list of every Egyptian king in hieroglyphs
a dictionary of hieroglyphs with their meanings in Latin
the Pyramid Texts written in Greek letters
questions.explanation: The stone repeats one decree of Ptolemy V in hieroglyphs, demotic script and Greek. Because scholars could read Greek, they could work out the other two. Jean-François Champollion announced his decipherment in 1822.

questions.stem: The Egyptian idea of maat refers to:
options: order, truth and justice, upheld by the king
the flood season of the River Nile
the red crown worn by the king of Lower Egypt
the spirit that left the body at death
questions.explanation: Maat was the cosmic order of truth, balance and justice that the king was responsible for maintaining against chaos (isfet). Upholding maat justified the king's absolute power.

questions.stem: Egyptian kingship in the Old Kingdom is described as theocratic because the king:
options: was elected by the priests of Re from among the leading nobles
ruled only in religious matters, while a council ran the state
shared power equally with an assembly of the nome governors
was believed to be a god, the living Horus, as well as the ruler
questions.explanation: In theocracy, religious and political authority are joined. The Egyptian king was the earthly form of Horus and, from the Fourth Dynasty, also ‘son of Re’, which made his rule absolute and sacred.

questions.stem: In Old Kingdom Egypt, the vizier was:
options: the governor in charge of a single province of Upper Egypt
the scribe who wrote the king's tomb inscriptions
the king's chief official, who oversaw the government
the high priest of the sun god at Heliopolis
questions.explanation: The vizier headed the bureaucracy, running the treasury, justice and public works on the king's behalf. Provincial governors were nomarchs, each responsible for one nome.

questions.stem: The nomarchs of Old Kingdom Egypt were:
options: workers who cut stone for the pyramids
governors of the provinces, called nomes
priests who tended the king's mortuary cult
soldiers who guarded the southern frontier
questions.explanation: Egypt was divided into provinces called nomes, each run by a nomarch who collected taxes, organised labour and kept order for the king.

questions.stem: The capital of Old Kingdom Egypt was Memphis, which was well placed because it lay:
options: where the Nile Valley meets the Delta, between the two lands
far in the south, close to the gold mines of the First Cataract
on the Mediterranean coast, the best harbour for trading ships
in the Western Desert, safe from the yearly flood of the Nile
questions.explanation: Memphis stood at the junction of Upper and Lower Egypt, near modern Cairo, a natural place to govern both. Its cemeteries at Saqqara and Giza hold many of the great pyramids.

questions.stem: Old Kingdom officials were paid with estates and goods from the king, and great pyramid projects drew labour from across Egypt. What does this show about the distribution of wealth?
options: Wealth was shared out equally among all Egyptians as fair payment for their labour
Peasants owned most of the land and paid nothing to the royal treasury
Temples held no land and depended entirely on gifts from ordinary farmers
Resources flowed to the state and were concentrated in the king and a small elite
questions.explanation: Taxes in grain, cattle and labour flowed to the king, who rewarded officials and priests with land and goods, so wealth was concentrated at the top. The peasants who farmed most of the land handed over much of its produce.

questions.stem: The Egyptian god of the dead and of rebirth, who ruled the underworld, was:
options: Osiris
Re
Horus
Seth
questions.explanation: Osiris was murdered by his brother Seth and brought back to life, becoming ruler of the dead. The dead king was identified with Osiris, while his living successor was Horus. Re was the sun god.

questions.stem: The cult of the sun god Re grew especially strong during the Fifth Dynasty. Which evidence shows this?
options: The cult of Osiris was banned throughout the whole country
Kings built sun temples and took the title ‘son of Re’
Kings stopped building any monuments for the dead
The capital moved from Memphis to Thebes in the south
questions.explanation: Fifth Dynasty kings built sun temples near Abusir, such as Niuserre's at Abu Gurob, and the ‘son of Re’ title became a standard part of royal names. Heliopolis was the centre of Re's cult. Memphis remained the capital.

questions.stem: Egyptians believed the ka, one part of a person's spirit, needed the body to survive and to receive food offerings. This belief explains:
options: the burial of the dead in unmarked graves
the scattering of ashes on the Nile flood
mummification and the offerings left at tombs
the burning of the dead on funeral pyres
questions.explanation: Because the ka needed a preserved body and continuing offerings, Egyptians developed mummification and set up offering places in tombs. Cremation would have destroyed the body the ka relied on.

questions.stem: In the Old Kingdom, the hope of joining the gods in the afterlife was mainly reserved for the king. By the First Intermediate Period, spells once used only for kings appeared on the coffins of officials. This change is best explained as:
options: a wider access to the afterlife as royal power weakened
a ban on royal burials imposed by the provincial nomarchs
the abandonment of belief in the god Osiris by the elite
the adoption of Mesopotamian beliefs about the underworld
questions.explanation: As central power declined, provincial elites adopted royal funerary texts and claimed an afterlife with Osiris for themselves, a change sometimes called the ‘democratisation of the afterlife’. Osiris became more, not less, important.

questions.stem: The first large monument built entirely of stone in Egypt was the Step Pyramid of:
options: Unas, at Abydos
Djoser, at Saqqara
Khufu, at Giza
Sneferu, at Dahshur
questions.explanation: The Step Pyramid of the Third Dynasty king Djoser at Saqqara was designed by his official Imhotep. It rose in six stages, like mastaba tombs stacked one on another.

questions.stem: Imhotep, who designed the Step Pyramid, was:
options: a priest of the god Osiris
an official of King Djoser
a king of the Fourth Dynasty
a nomarch of Upper Egypt
questions.explanation: Imhotep was a high official under Djoser and is credited with the Step Pyramid. Later Egyptians revered him as a sage and eventually as a god of healing.

questions.stem: The Bent Pyramid at Dahshur changes angle partway up. The most widely accepted explanation is that:
options: the king died, so his son finished it in a different style of his own choosing
it was designed to point at two different stars in the night sky
the top was added centuries later by Middle Kingdom restorers
the builders reduced the angle to stop the structure becoming unstable
questions.explanation: Cracking and settling during construction seem to have led Sneferu's builders to lower the angle of the upper part. Sneferu then built the Red Pyramid, the first successful true pyramid, at a gentler angle.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows the development of pyramid design in the correct order?
options: Step Pyramid of Djoser, Bent Pyramid, Great Pyramid of Khufu
Great Pyramid of Khufu, Step Pyramid of Djoser, Bent Pyramid
Bent Pyramid, Great Pyramid of Khufu, Step Pyramid of Djoser
Step Pyramid of Djoser, Great Pyramid of Khufu, Bent Pyramid
questions.explanation: Djoser's step pyramid came first, in the Third Dynasty. Sneferu experimented with the Meidum, Bent and Red pyramids early in the Fourth Dynasty, and his son Khufu then built the Great Pyramid at Giza.

questions.stem: The Meidum Pyramid began as a step pyramid and was later given a smooth outer casing, which partly collapsed. Its significance is that it shows:
options: the change from step pyramids to true pyramids during the early Fourth Dynasty
that the Egyptians gave up pyramid building after the Third Dynasty ended
that true pyramids were built before any step pyramid had been tried
that kings of the Old Kingdom were buried only in rock-cut cliff tombs
questions.explanation: Meidum, linked with Huni and Sneferu, was converted from a stepped form to a smooth-sided one, a key moment in the move to the true pyramid. Its partial collapse shows builders were still learning.

questions.stem: The three main pyramids at Giza were built for:
options: Djoser, Sneferu and Unas
Narmer, Aha and Djer
Teti, Pepi I and Pepi II
Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure
questions.explanation: The Fourth Dynasty kings Khufu, his son Khafre and Menkaure built the Giza pyramids. The Great Sphinx is part of Khafre's complex. Djoser's and Unas's pyramids are at Saqqara.

questions.stem: Excavations near the Giza pyramids uncovered workers' houses, bakeries and tombs of workers buried with offerings close to the pyramids. These finds challenge the popular view that:
options: the pyramids were built over a period of many decades
the pyramids were built by large numbers of slaves
the pyramids were built for kings of the Fourth Dynasty
the pyramids were built using stone from Egyptian quarries
questions.explanation: Organised housing, food supplies and honourable burials near the king suggest skilled workers and rotating labour crews organised by the state, not slaves. The other statements are supported by the evidence rather than challenged by it.

questions.stem: The Pyramid Texts first appear carved inside the pyramid of Unas at Saqqara. They are:
options: records of the workers and supplies used to build the pyramid
laws issued by the king for the governors of the provinces
letters sent by the king to the rulers of foreign lands
spells to help the dead king reach the afterlife among the gods
questions.explanation: The Pyramid Texts are the oldest religious texts of Egypt: spells and hymns to protect the king and help him ascend to the sky and join Re and Osiris. They were carved in the burial chambers of late Old Kingdom pyramids.

questions.stem: In the Old Kingdom, officials and nobles were usually buried in:
options: pyramids of the same size as the king's own pyramid
rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings at Thebes
simple pit graves in the desert with no grave goods
mastaba tombs in cemeteries near the king's pyramid
questions.explanation: Nobles built rectangular mastaba tombs, often clustered around the king's pyramid at Giza and Saqqara, showing their status came from serving him. The Valley of the Kings was used in the New Kingdom.

questions.stem: The scenes of farming, fishing and crafts painted and carved in Old Kingdom nobles' tombs at Saqqara are useful evidence. What is their main limitation?
options: They show only the king himself, so they tell us nothing about any other social group
They were added by archaeologists in the nineteenth century to attract visitors
They show an ideal, everlasting world for the owner, not daily life as it really was
They were painted by foreign artists who had never visited Egypt's farms and towns
questions.explanation: Tomb scenes were meant to provide the owner with an abundant afterlife, so they present an idealised picture: plentiful harvests, obedient workers and no hardship. They still show tools, activities and occupations that are valuable evidence.

questions.stem: The statue of Khafre seated on his throne, with the falcon god Horus behind his head, best expresses:
options: the king's role as a priest of the god Osiris
the king's defeat of enemies in Lower Egypt
the king's humility before the nomarchs
the king's divine protection and lasting authority
questions.explanation: Horus spreading his wings behind Khafre's head shows the king as the god's earthly form and under his protection. The calm, idealised pose in hard stone was meant to last for eternity.

questions.stem: Egyptian artists of the Old Kingdom showed important people larger than others in the same scene. This convention is called:
options: realistic portraiture
hierarchical scale
perspective drawing
foreshortening
questions.explanation: Hierarchical scale shows status through size, so kings and tomb owners tower over servants and family. Egyptian art avoided perspective and foreshortening, showing figures with head in profile and torso from the front.

questions.stem: Late in the Old Kingdom, the nomarchs became more powerful. Which development shows this?
options: They were moved each year between provinces so they could not build local power
They were all buried in the king's own pyramid as a sign of their high favour
They lost the right to collect taxes, which passed to the priests of Re instead
Their offices became hereditary and they built rich tombs in their own provinces
questions.explanation: By the Sixth Dynasty many nomarchs passed their posts to their sons and were buried in their own provinces rather than near the king, showing local loyalties and wealth. Revenue that once went to Memphis stayed in the provinces.

questions.stem: Which combination of causes do historians most often give for the collapse of central power at the end of the Old Kingdom?
options: The conquest of Egypt by Assyria and the deportation of its officials
A rebellion by the pyramid builders, who refused to keep working for King Pepi II
Growing power of the nomarchs, a weakened treasury and a run of low Nile floods
A Hyksos invasion of the Delta and the loss of the capital at Memphis
questions.explanation: Wealth diverted to nomarchs and temples, the very long reign of Pepi II and evidence of low floods and famine all weakened the monarchy. The Hyksos arrived much later, at the end of the Middle Kingdom, and Assyria invaded Egypt about a thousand years after that.

questions.stem: During the First Intermediate Period, rival dynasties ruled from:
options: Herakleopolis in the north and Thebes in the south
Memphis in the north and Avaris in the eastern Delta
Babylon in the east and Thebes in the south
Giza in the north and Hierakonpolis in the south
questions.explanation: Kings at Herakleopolis (Ninth and Tenth dynasties) and at Thebes (Eleventh Dynasty) competed for control until the Theban Mentuhotep II reunited Egypt. Avaris was the later Hyksos capital.
